key_insight: Giving novices access to LLMs measurably improves their performance on a range of in silico biology tasks compared with internet-only resources, but this uplift also amplifies certain dual-use risks that warrant mitigation and policy attention.
problem_solved: Clarifies whether LLMs actually 'uplift' novice human performance on biosecurity-relevant computational biology tasks and quantifies the tradeoff between scientific acceleration and increased dual-use potential.
method: Controlled human study: novices were randomized to either LLM-assisted or internet-only conditions.
Multi-model, multi-benchmark evaluation across eight biosecurity-relevant in silico task sets, measuring task accuracy, time, and user strategies.
Cross-cutting analysis of benefit (performance uplift) and risk (instances where LLM access made sensitive tasks easier or more likely).
impact: Provides empirical evidence for AI/ML practitioners and policymakers about how LLM deployment affects novice capability and dual-use exposure, informing safer model releases, access controls, and benchmark design.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing average task performance: LLM-assisted vs internet-only across the eight task sets.
Study flow diagram showing randomization, conditions (LLM vs internet), and measured outcomes (accuracy, time, qualitative notes).
Risk–Benefit quadrant or scatterplot mapping each task by magnitude of uplift (benefit) versus dual-use risk (concern).
Icon strip summarizing key takeaways: net uplift, variance by task, policy implications, suggested mitigations.
paper_title: LLM Novice Uplift on Dual-Use, In Silico Biology Tasks
paper_authors: Chen Bo Calvin Zhang, Christina Q. Knight, Nicholas Kruus, Jason Hausenloy, Pedro Medeiros
